new: The Minzhu Road neighbourhood committee was on the ground floor of a three-storey building. At a table by the door a woman in a red armband took both their temperatures and had them write their names in a book.

old: Officer Wang sat by the window, about fifty, a black padded vest over his uniform, a thermos cup in front of him. new: Officer Wang sat by the window, fifty or so, a thermos in front of him. Beside him stood a young auxiliary officer. The sub-district office had sent a woman in her thirties, in glasses, holding a notebook. The neighbourhood grid worker sat by the door.

old: She said the child had been rebellious since she was small, wouldn’t be told, couldn’t stand being at home, looked down on the family for being poor, for not being well off. She said the minute the holidays came she was off out, and she and the girl’s dad had tried every way of talking to her, and she just wouldn’t listen. She said over New Year her dad stood at the door every day waiting, till midnight. She said with the epidemic this bad, a sixteen-year-old girl out there on her own, what was she eating and drinking, where was she living, if anything happened what would they say to her dead—“to her real mum,” she corrected herself.
new: “This child’s been rebellious ever since she was small. Won’t be told, can’t stay put at home, thinks the family’s too poor, thinks the house isn’t good enough, and the minute there’s a holiday she’s off. Her dad and I have talked to her till we’re blue in the face and she just won’t listen,” she said. “Over New Year her dad stood at the door every single day waiting, waiting till midnight. With the epidemic this bad, a sixteen-year-old girl out there on her own—what’s she eating, what’s she drinking, where’s she living? If something were to happen, how would we answer to her late—to her birth mother?”

old: A room of twenty-odd square metres, a long table with four chairs on each side, the table covered in dark green baize under a sheet of glass. On the wall hung a scroll, “Harmony is most precious,” in a glass frame with a water stain in one corner. On the windowsill was a pothos, half its leaves yellow.
new: A room of twenty-odd square metres, one long table with four chairs down each side. On the wall hung a piece of calligraphy, “Harmony above all.” On the windowsill was a pot of pothos, half its leaves yellow.

old: The mediator was called Ma, in his sixties; before retiring he had worked at the sub-district office for thirty years, and everyone called him Director Ma. He wore a grey sweater with a navy jacket over it, and pinned to the front of the jacket a badge reading “People’s Mediator.” He poured everyone a cup of tea, the very cheap kind of green tea that brews up yellowish.
new: The mediator’s name was Ma, sixty-something, thirty years at the sub-district office before he retired, and everyone called him Director Ma. He poured each of them a cup of tea.

old: They got there at five past three. There was hardly anyone in the hall, just an old woman jabbing at the ticket machine and getting nothing out of it. The security guard came over and pressed it for her, handed her a little slip, and she held the slip and read the number on it aloud, one character at a time.
new: It was five past three when they got there, and the hall was nearly empty.

old: When they came out of the bank, the sun was already sinking west. The March sun had no strength in it; it shone on the street, on the concrete where the snow had just melted, glaring.

She didn’t understand. She didn’t know when “before” was, who “a lot of people” were, what “the way they look at you” looked like. But she looked at his profile, and when he said “a lot,” the muscle along his jaw moved.
new: “When your ‘before’ was, who the ‘lot of people’ are, what that look is like, I don’t understand a single bit of it,” she said. “But when you said ‘a lot,’ your whole jaw went tight, right here.”

old: “…Mm,” she said.
new: “…Did it,” he said.

old: The customer-service back end was a web page: a column of conversations on the left, the chat box on the right, and along the top a row of red numbers, the unanswered messages. She propped her phone on a stack of textbooks on her desk; the computer was her dad’s old laptop, which took three minutes to boot and whose fan sounded like a hairdryer when it got going. While her two brothers were in their online classes, the computer was hers.
new: The customer-service back end was a web page: a column of conversations on the left, the chat box on the right, and along the top a row of red numbers, the messages not yet answered. The computer was her dad’s old laptop; while her two brothers were in online classes, it was hers.

old: Her parents’ attitude to this job started out as “signing a contract is a good thing,” and slowly turned into something else.

On the bridge over the river, now the checkpoint was gone, you had to wear a mask to cross, and at the end of the bridge stood an old man in a red armband who shouted at anyone without one. Su Tang rode her old bike with the flower rolls and the cabbage in the basket and a case of milk tied to the back with string, her mask on tight, and as she crossed the bridge the wind got in round the edges of the mask and made her eyes stream.
new: The checkpoint on the bridge over the river had gone, but an old man in a red armband still stood at the end of it and shouted at anyone without a mask. Su Tang rode her old bicycle with flower rolls and spicy pickled cabbage in the basket and a crate of milk tied on the back.

old: There were a few more people on Back Street than last week. The copy shop was open; the braised-meat stall wasn’t out yet. The internet café’s curtain was hooked up, and two boys stood at the door in masks smoking, masks pulled down under their chins: a drag, mask up, another drag, mask down.

Su Tang went up, knocked, and the door opened. The moment she was inside she took off her mask, and the smell of cat fur and cat litter and the dry heat baked out by the electric heater all came rushing at her.
new: Su Tang went upstairs and knocked, and the door opened. The moment she was inside she took her mask off.

old: He was wearing a grey hoodie, the same one he had on when she came the day before yesterday, a tuft of cat fur stuck to the cuff, which had been stuck there the day before yesterday too. On the counter were three instant-noodle tubs stacked one inside another, the fork still stuck in the top one. He had headphones on, in a meeting; when he heard the door he raised one hand and waved at her, then put it down again, his eyes not leaving the screen.
new: He was wearing a grey hoodie, the same one he’d had on when she came the day before yesterday, with a cat hair stuck to the cuff that had been stuck there the day before yesterday too. Three instant-noodle tubs were stacked on the bar. He had earphones in and was in a meeting; hearing the door, he lifted a hand and waved it at her without taking his eyes off the screen.

old: With the rest of the money he bought a new pair of trainers, bought three game season passes, and the moment the internet café opened, topped up five hundred on a membership. He also treated the internet café gang to barbecue twice; the barbecue stall had only come out at the end of March, and the owner wore his mask hooked over one ear and coughed as he grilled, coughed so much that Huang Yingjun shifted his stool back half a metre.
new: With the rest of the money he bought a new pair of trainers and three season passes for games, put five hundred yuan on a membership the minute the internet café reopened, and treated the internet café lot to barbecue twice.

old: Two turns in from Back Street, the side of an old building. Su Tang stood there looking at the seven steps going down; at the bottom was an iron door, most of its paint gone, rusted out in reddish-brown patches. Beside the door was a little window with its sill level with the pavement; she looked down at it, and the glass was coated in a layer of dust, so she couldn’t see inside.
new: Two turnings in from Back Street, the side of an old building. Seven steps led down to an iron door with most of its paint gone. Beside the door was a small window, its sill level with the pavement.

old: The bottles filled four big bags. The noodle tubs filled one. Su Tang poured the half pot of noodle soup down the toilet and flushed it, scrubbed the electric pot three times, until the black scorched mark on the bottom had at last faded a little. She swept, mopped, diluted the 84 with water and wiped down the corners and under the bed.
new: The bottles filled four big bags, the noodle tubs one. Su Tang poured away that half-pot of noodle soup, scrubbed the electric pot three times, swept the floor, mopped it, diluted the 84 disinfectant and wiped down the corners and under the bed.

old: Su Tang said nothing. She looked at Gu Xuerong’s profile, at the way she chewed the tangerine, very slowly, one bite after another, as if chewing something perfectly ordinary.
new: “Xuerong, when you say all this, how come it sounds like you’re talking about somebody else’s family?” said Su Tang.

old: “She believes in another thing too,” said Gu Xuerong. “It’s called Three Redemptions Christ.”
new: “Say it enough times and it turns into somebody else’s family,” said Gu Xuerong. “There’s one more thing she believes in. It’s called Three Redemptions Christ.”

old: Su Tang sat on the edge of that bed for a long time.
new: Su Tang sat on the edge of that bed for a good while.

old: She thought of her mum. Her mum believed in things a bit too: burned incense at New Year, went to the temple on the first and fifteenth to kowtow. When she was little and had a fever, her mum went to the temple for a charm too and stuck it at the head of her bed. But after she got the charm, her mum still carried her to the county hospital, went to A&E, sat up all night in the corridor, and the next day her eyes were swollen like two peaches.
new: “My mum believes in this stuff too,” she said. “Incense at New Year, off to the temple to kowtow on the first and the fifteenth. When I had a fever as a little kid she went to the temple and got a paper charm as well, and came back and stuck it over my bed. But once she’d got the charm, she still carried me to the county hospital, went through A&E, and sat up all night in the corridor, and the next day her eyes were swollen like two peaches.”

old: Her mum had never said she’d come to collect a debt.
new: She sniffed. “She has never once said I came to collect a debt.”

old: That afternoon, Su Tang carried the four big bags of bottles and threw them one by one into the rubbish point at the end of Back Street. Crouched beside the rubbish point was an old man who collected scrap, in a grey cloth mask, and when he saw her throwing bottles away he jumped up and said don’t throw them, don’t throw them, give them to me.
new: That afternoon Su Tang carried the four big bags of bottles to the rubbish station at the mouth of Back Street. An old scrap collector was squatting beside it, and when he saw she was about to throw bottles away he jumped up and said don’t throw them, don’t throw them, give them here, give them here.

old: The old man stamped them flat one by one, crunch, crunch, and when he’d stamped them he put them into his own woven sack. Four big bags took him nearly twenty minutes. When he was done, he took two yuan out of his pocket and tried to give it to her.
new: The old man stamped them flat one by one and packed them into his own woven sack, and when he had finished he took two yuan out of his pocket and tried to give it to her.

old: Close up, she could see his eyes were full of red veins, two dark bluish-black marks under them. The screen had several windows open: one of code, one a spreadsheet, one a chat app with a dozen conversations flashing, and one the Town Matters back end, the number in its top right corner red.
new: Only up close could she see it clearly: Ye Zhixing’s eyes were bloodshot all over, with two blue-black patches under them. Several windows were open on his screen: code, a spreadsheet, a dozen flashing chats, and the City Matters back end, the number in its top right corner in red.

old: Rice Cake first. It wriggled free of Ye Zhixia’s arms, jumped onto the sofa, trod a few circles on Ye Zhixing’s stomach, so that he grunted in his sleep, and then settled down, curled into a ginger-and-white ball, weighing on the pit of his stomach.
new: First came Rice Cake. It wriggled out of Ye Zhixia’s arms, jumped onto the sofa, trod a few circles on Ye Zhixing’s stomach and settled, right on top of his belly.

old: Then Calico, down from the back of the sofa, burrowing into the gap between his arm and his body, squeezing until the gap was a bit bigger, and lying in it.
new: Then the calico, who burrowed into the gap between his arm and his body. The Devon, which hated the cold, curled into the hollow of his neck with its head on his collarbone.

old: Then the Devon. The Devon had always felt the cold, and in winter went looking for the warmest spot. It sniffed at the side of Ye Zhixing’s neck, smelled something, its big ears twitched, and then it curled up in the hollow of his neck, its head resting on his collarbone.

Blue-and-White jumped up and lay on his shins. The American Shorthair lay on his feet. The British Blue turned three circles on his knees, couldn’t find a spot, and in the end lay down on top of Blue-and-White, who didn’t object.
new: Blue-and-White lay on his shins, the American Shorthair on his feet, and the blue British Shorthair, finding no room, ended up lying on top of Blue-and-White.

old: Your Highness came last. It walked out through the sliding door to the back room—which it had opened itself—came to the sofa, looked up, looked at the pile of cats, looked at the person underneath, and then jumped up onto the back of the sofa and lay down in the spot above Ye Zhixing’s head, its long tail hanging down so it rested exactly across his forehead.
new: Your Highness came last. It pawed open the sliding door of the inner room by itself, walked out, jumped onto the back of the sofa and lay down above Ye Zhixing’s head, its long tail hanging down to rest exactly on his forehead.

old: The queue stretched all the way to the breakfast stall across the road. Each student had to stand a metre from the next; circles had been painted on the ground in red, one after another, and you stood in a circle, and when you moved up one, you stepped into the next circle. At the gate there was a table with two teachers behind it, one with a thermometer gun, one with a register; the gun beeped, a number was read out, 36.3, 36.5, 36.1, and the register got a tick.
new: The queue ran all the way to the door of the breakfast shop opposite. Circles had been painted on the ground in red, one after another; you stood in a circle, and when the line moved you stepped into the next. At the gate were two teachers, one with a thermometer gun and one with a register: a beep, a number called out, a mark made.

old: At Ye Zhixia’s school, they said, you also had to wash your hands: a row of taps just inside the gate, and you had to scrub for a full twenty seconds before they let you in. No. 8 High didn’t have that; at No. 8 High’s gate there was just a bottle of hand sanitizer, one pump, rub, in you go.

Everyone wore a mask. Mostly blue surgical ones, some white, some black, a few girls in pink ones printed with little flowers, and one boy in an N95, the metal strip over his nose pressed down tight, his voice coming out muffled.
new: Everyone had a mask on. One boy was in an N95 with the metal strip pinched tight over the bridge of his nose, and it made his voice come out muffled and nasal.

old: The desks in the classroom had been pulled apart: before it had been two to a desk, now it was one each, with a bit of space in front, behind and to the sides. Forty-odd desks packed the classroom full; the back row was pushed right up against the blackboard newspaper.

Three months of online classes at home: you attended, then you stopped attending; you attended, then you fell asleep. Body clocks were long since wrecked, two or three in the morning to bed, up at noon, and now you had to be at school by six-thirty, with morning reading at seven, and halfway through the reading heads started drooping. People held out through the first lesson; in the second lesson someone put their head down; by the third a whole patch of heads were down.
new: After three months of online classes everyone’s body clock was a wreck: asleep at two or three in the morning, up at noon. Now they had to be at school by half past six. First period people could still hold out; in second period heads started going down; by third period a whole swathe was down.

old: So he taught during evening study.
new: “So how are you running that class of yours now?” Ye Zhixing asked him.

old: The method was simple. Evening study was for doing your own homework, and if there was something you couldn’t do, you could ask. The teacher on duty sat at the front marking, and didn’t usually bother with anything. Chen Xi sat in the row by the window; when someone brought over a paper to ask, he explained. When he’d explained, the person went back and carried on writing. Money wasn’t handed over in the classroom: there was a teacher on duty, and phones weren’t allowed—though everyone had one.
new: “In evening study, where else,” said Chen Xi. “Evening study’s for doing your own homework, right, and if you’re stuck you can ask. I sit in the row by the window. Whoever comes over with a paper, I explain it, and when I’m done they go back and carry on. People sneak over from Class Three and Class Eight too and queue at the back door, and every time I finish one, another one comes in.”

old: He could get through a dozen or more people a night. People from Class Three and Class Eight slipped over too, standing at Class Seven’s back door, poking their heads in, waiting for him to finish one so the next could come in.
new: “And the teacher on duty just lets you?”

old: The teacher on duty looked up a few times, and saw a group of students crowded round one student, holding papers, going through problems, maths and physics, very seriously, someone sometimes drawing a diagram with a pen on scrap paper. That’s a good thing, the teacher thought. And went back to marking.
new: “He’s looked up quite a few times,” said Chen Xi. “What he sees is a bunch of students crowded round one student going through maths problems, with someone drawing diagrams. He thinks that’s a good thing, so he puts his head down and goes back to his marking.”

old: The money was transferred in the toilets.
new: “And the money? Aren’t phones banned in the classroom?”

old: “You crafty little sod,” Ye Zhixing said when he heard.
new: “Everybody’s got one on them. The money gets sent in the toilets.”
“You’re a sly one, aren’t you.”

old: That upstairs room, which before the epidemic was packed every afternoon, now got two or three customers in an afternoon, all middle-schoolers from nearby who dropped in after school to sit for a while, stroke the cats, order a drink, and left within the hour. Old Zhou was back, but the griddle barely got fired up a few times a day; most of the time he sat at the kitchen door in his mask looking at his phone, short videos, laughing to himself.
new: The second floor that used to be packed by afternoon before the epidemic now got two or three customers in an afternoon, and they left within the hour. Old Zhou was back, but the griddle was fired up only a few times a day, and most of the time he sat by the kitchen door in his mask, scrolling short videos and laughing to himself.

old: Now and then there was a delivery order. Mostly omurice; on Meituan, Ye Zhixia had given it a picture of Rice Cake lying next to a plate of omurice, Rice Cake’s video was still being shared, and some people ordered delivery just for that picture. When the delivery rider came to pick up, he stood at the door, poked his head in, and asked: “Where’s the fat cat?”
new: Now and then there was a delivery order, usually omurice. When the rider came to collect it he would stand in the doorway, crane his neck in and ask, “Where’s that fat cat?”

old: That evening, Ye Zhixing took a screenshot of the numbers in the back end and looked at it for a good while.
new: That evening Big Liu sent him a voice message, with the baby crying in the background.

old: Then he leaned back in his chair and let out a long breath.
new: “Boss, have you looked at the dashboard? The four games together went over three thousand today.”
“I saw.”
“So next month’s wages…”
“Paid as normal, every penny. There’s enough for the next six months,” said Ye Zhixing. “Let Xiaowen and the others know too, so everybody knows where they stand.”
He leaned back in his chair and let out a long breath.

old: Enough. For the next six months at least, enough.
Gu Xuerong didn’t answer.
new: “What happens later can wait till later,” said Gu Xuerong. “Right now they can’t find me, so right now it’s fine.”
“Being able to see the end isn’t so bad, actually,” said Gu Xuerong. “I can’t even see where the end is.”

old: “What about you? Have you thought about later?”
new: “…So you’ve really never thought about later?”

old: Her routine was very regular now. A month and more in the village, in bed by half past nine every night along with her grandparents; back in the county town, she had brought the habit with her: wash at ten, in bed at ten-twenty, lights out at half past ten—the light being the little lamp at the head of her own bed—and she pulled the quilt over her head, said “night, Xuerong,” and within five minutes her breathing had slowed.
new: She kept very regular hours now. After more than a month in the village going to bed when her grandparents did, she washed at ten, was in bed at ten-twenty, and at half past ten switched off the little lamp at the head of her bed, pulled the quilt over her head and said “Night, Xuerong,” and in under five minutes her breathing had lengthened.

old: “Then take me.”
new: “Then take me along with you.”
